summary: Trump showed his hand in April — he is sensitive to market reactions and will reverse course if tariffs are clearly not working, providing a downside circuit breaker.
summary_extended: Baker argues that Trump's April 2025 tariff reversal — when markets reacted sharply negative and Trump backed down — revealed a meaningful behavioral pattern: Trump is sensitive to market pressure and will change course when economic pain becomes visible. Baker frames this not as ideological flexibility but as a practical circuit breaker, suggesting that extreme downside scenarios from tariff escalation are partially capped by Trump's demonstrated responsiveness to market signals. The key uncertainty Baker identifies is not whether Trump will eventually reverse course, but whether he can do so quickly enough to prevent serious economic damage if conditions deteriorate rapidly. This is a macro risk management observation rather than a directional trade — it implies investors should not price in the most catastrophic tariff outcomes as highly probable, but should remain watchful of the speed of any future policy response.
detail: Baker notes that Trump 'looked into the abyss' in April and demonstrated willingness to change course when markets reacted negatively. He views this as a meaningful risk management signal — the key question is whether he can change quickly enough if things deteriorate. He frames Trump as 'responsive' rather than ideologically rigid on tariffs.
confidence_evidence: Baker makes this point carefully and hedges with 'if it's not working, does he change quickly enough.' Moderate conviction — it's a risk management observation, not a strong directional call.
